Definition and Function
The esophagus is a muscular, hollow tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach. It plays a crucial role in the digestive system by
transporting ingested food and liquids via peristalsis, a coordinated wave-like muscular contraction.
Location and General Features
●
●
●
The esophagus is about 25 cm long in adults.
It begins at the level of the C6 vertebra (cricoid cartilage) and extends to the T11 vertebra, where it joins the stomach at the
gastroesophageal junction.
It passes through the diaphragm via the esophageal hiatus at the T10 level.
Relations to Other Structures
●
●
●
Anteriorly: The trachea (in the cervical and upper thoracic regions), left atrium (in the lower thoracic region).
Posteriorly: The vertebral column.
Laterally: The carotid arteries, vagus nerves, and thoracic aorta.

The oesophagus
Physiological Role
●
●
The esophagus functions solely as a conduit; it does not participate in digestion or absorption.
It contains two sphincters:
1.
Upper esophageal sphincter (UES) – prevents air from entering the esophagus during breathing.
2.
Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) – prevents reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus.
Clinical Importance
Understanding the anatomy of the esophagus is crucial in clinical practice, particularly in conditions like:
●
●
●
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) – dysfunction of the LES.
Achalasia – failure of the LES to relax.
Esophageal cancer – one of the most aggressive gastrointestinal malignancies.
